common_name: Black Jack Agapanthus (Everpanthus Series, RHS Chelsea Plant of the Year 2023)

planting.note: Set out divisions or potted plants after frost danger passes, into fertile, moist but well-drained soil or large containers.

directions: This evergreen agapanthus produces rounded flowerheads packed with far more florets than typical cultivars, opening from near-black buds into deep purple-black blooms that take on a metallic sheen as they age, with a bloom season roughly twice as long as older varieties. Grow it in a sunny, sheltered spot or a large pot of peat-free compost, since the clump resents waterlogging but also dislikes drying out completely during active growth. In colder regions, move containers to a frost-free spot or mulch heavily over winter, as this selection is less cold-tolerant than hardy Agapanthus africanus types. Divide congested clumps in spring just as new growth emerges.
sources: RHS Chelsea Flower Show Plant of the Year 2023

common_name: Destiny Semponium (Hardy Aeonium-Sempervivum Hybrid, RHS Chelsea Plant of the Year 2022)

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets or cuttings in sharply drained, gritty soil or containers once hard frosts have passed.

directions: An intergeneric cross between Aeonium and Sempervivum, this rosette-forming succulent holds its deep purple, veined foliage year-round and keeps growing through winter without the dormancy typical of its Aeonium parent. In the growing season it sends up tall, chandelier-like stems topped with starry yellow flowers with reddish centers. Site it in full sun or light shade in very free-draining, gritty compost, whether in a container or a rockery, and water sparingly since soggy roots are its main vulnerability. It tolerates light frost but should be given winter cover or brought under glass where temperatures drop much below freezing for extended periods.
sources: RHS Chelsea Flower Show Plant of the Year 2022

common_name: Starlight Flowering Cherry (RHS Chelsea Plant of the Year 2024)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in autumn or early spring into any well-drained garden soil in full sun.

directions: Bred from a cross between an edible red-fruited cherry and the autumn-flowering Prunus subhirtella 'Autumnalis Rosea', this compact deciduous tree produces clusters of fragrant, star-shaped white flowers with narrow, slender petals in early spring, and often repeats with a lighter flush of bloom in autumn. Its upright, bushy habit and modest ultimate size make it well suited to smaller gardens where larger flowering cherries would overwhelm the space. Grow it in full sun in any reasonably drained soil, and prune only lightly after flowering to maintain shape, since cherries heal poorly from heavy cuts. It tolerates a wide range of soils and is fully winter-hardy once established.
sources: RHS Chelsea Flower Show Plant of the Year 2024

common_name: Petite Perfume Pink Mock Orange (First Pink-Flowered Philadelphus, RHS Chelsea Plant of the Year 2025)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in autumn or spring into moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Bred by Alan Postill, this compact mock orange was the first of its kind to open genuinely pink flowers rather than the white blooms typical of the genus, with deep pink buds opening to fragrant flowers that fade toward the petal edges while keeping dark pink centers. Its naturally tidy, rounded habit stays within bounds without regular pruning, making it a good fit for smaller borders or mixed plantings where larger mock oranges would need constant cutting back. Grow it in full sun for the heaviest bloom, though it tolerates partial shade, in any moderately fertile soil that drains well. Established plants are fully hardy and need only an occasional thinning of old wood right after flowering to stay vigorous.
sources: RHS Chelsea Flower Show Plant of the Year 2025

common_name: Red Ninja Hosta (Purple-Red Foliage with Purple Flowers, RHS Chelsea Plant of the Year 2026)

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted hostas in spring into humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in dappled shade.

directions: Bred by Ninja Kramer, this distinctive hosta carries deep purple-red leaves rimmed in green, a striking departure from the blue, gold, and plain green tones most hostas offer, and sends up purple flower spikes from late summer into early autumn. It stays compact enough for mixed borders, raised beds, or large containers on a patio or balcony. Give it gentle morning sun rather than deep shade to bring out the strongest foliage color, paired with consistently moist, well-drained soil rich in organic matter. It is exceptionally cold-hardy for the genus and needs little care beyond slug control and an annual mulch to conserve soil moisture.
sources: RHS Chelsea Flower Show Plant of the Year 2026
